entry.title: How rare is a 17-0 NFL season? The math behind a perfect season
entry.summary:
Every NFL fan knows the 1972 Miami Dolphins are the only team to finish a season perfect. How hard is that, really? A little probability gives a surprisingly clear answer. If a team wins each game with the same probability p, and games are treated as independent, the chance of winning all 17 is simply: P(17-0) = p^17 Here is what that looks like for different per-game win probabilities:
Win probability per game (p) P(17-0) = p^17 Roughly 1 in...
0.60 0.017% 5,900
0.70 0.23% 430
0.80 2.25% 44
0.85 6.31% 16
0.90 16.68% 6
Even a team that is an 85% favorite in every single game (which no real team is) goes 17-0 only about once in 16 tries. Small drops in per-game probability compound fast: moving from 0.90 to 0.80 cuts the perfect-season chance by about 7x. 1972 Dolphins: 14-0 in the regular season, then three playoff wins including the Super Bowl, for a 17-0 record overall. That is the only perfect season, playoffs included, in the Super Bowl era. 2007 Patriots: 16-0 in the regular season, but they lost Super Bowl XLII, so they did not finish 18-0. Today's regular season is 17 games, so a "17-0" regular season is a different (and in some ways easier) target than the Dolphins' 17-0, which included the playoffs. The independence assumption is a simplification. Real games are correlated (injuries, schedule strength, a quarterback who is available or not), and p is different each week. But the p^17 estimate is a good back-of-the-envelope tool for seeing why perfect seasons are so rare. If you want to play with the idea, you can build a roster and see how close you can get to 17-0 in 17-0 Game, a free browser NFL roster and season challenge. What per-game win probability would you assign to the best team you have ever seen?

entry.title: Layer 2 Scaling Solutions
entry.summary: Layer 2 scaling solutions help blockchains like Ethereum process more activity without forcing every transaction to happen directly on the base chain. Ethereum’s main network is secure and decentralized, but blockspace is limited. When demand rises, fees increase and users can get priced out. Layer 2s address this by moving transaction activity to scaling systems that sit around Ethereum while still using it for settlement, security, data posting, or verification. The most important Layer 2 designs today are rollups. Rollups process transactions off-chain, bundle them together, and post data or proofs back to Ethereum. This makes transactions cheaper and faster while keeping a connection to Ethereum’s trust foundation.
